23:1.prayer: Father, keep me steady in every setting. When status or influence impresses me, anchor me in Your approval and give me clear eyes to see what is really before me. Amen.

23:2.devotion: This striking image uses deliberate exaggeration: if your appetites rule you, restrain yourself forcefully before the temptations of a grand setting. It is vivid wisdom poetry about self-control, urging us to govern our desires rather than letting desire govern us.
23:2.reflection: Where does my appetite—whether for food, pleasure, or approval—override my better judgment?
23:2.action: Choose one appetite today and practice deliberate restraint, setting a clear limit before you begin.
23:2.prayer: Lord, You made me with desires, but You call me to master them. Give me strength to say no to myself when indulgence would lead me astray, and fill me with what truly satisfies. Amen.

23:3.devotion: The ruler's delicacies are called deceptive food because they come with strings attached—flattery now, obligation later. What looks generous and free often carries hidden costs. Wisdom looks past the surface of every offer to see what is truly being asked in return.
23:3.reflection: Do I examine the hidden strings attached to attractive offers before accepting them?
23:3.action: When an appealing offer comes today, ask what will be expected of you in return before responding.
23:3.prayer: Father, give me discernment to see beyond the surface. Guard me from gifts that carry hidden costs, and help me value integrity above every tempting convenience. Amen.

23:4.devotion: This proverb does not condemn diligent work, which Scripture elsewhere honors. It warns against exhausting ourselves in the relentless pursuit of wealth, trusting our own cleverness to secure riches. Wisdom keeps labor in its place and rests in God rather than in earnings.
23:4.reflection: Is my drive for success crowding out rest, relationships, and trust in God?
23:4.action: Set a firm stopping point on your work today and honor it, using the reclaimed time for rest or people you love.
23:4.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times I strive as if everything depends on me. Teach me to work faithfully and then rest, trusting You with the outcomes I cannot control. Amen.

23:5.devotion: Riches, this proverb says, sprout wings. Wealth is fleeting—it can vanish through loss, change, or circumstances beyond our control. Fixing our eyes on money means gazing at something that will not stay. Lasting security is found in God, not in shifting treasure.
23:5.reflection: How much of my peace of mind rests on things that could fly away tomorrow?
23:5.action: Name one thing you own or earn that you are clinging to, and thank God for it while consciously holding it loosely.
23:5.prayer: Father, keep my heart anchored in You, the only security that never flies away. Free me from anxieties about wealth, and make me generous with what You have entrusted to me. Amen.

23:6.devotion: The miser's hospitality is hollow. He counts every cost even as he offers food, and his grudging heart poisons the meal. This proverb warns against attaching ourselves to people whose generosity is reluctant, because what they give comes wrapped in resentment and expectation.
23:6.reflection: Do I give freely, or does a stingy, calculating spirit creep into my generosity?
23:6.action: Give something today—a meal, help, or encouragement—with no expectation of return or acknowledgment.
23:6.prayer: Lord, make my heart cheerful in giving, not grudging or calculating. Guard me from sour hospitality, and let my generosity reflect Your own open-handed kindness to me. Amen.

23:7.devotion: Within a warning about stingy hosts, this proverb observes that outward generosity can mask an inward reality. The person says "eat and drink," but his reluctant heart tells the truth. What we treasure and dwell on within shapes who we truly are, regardless of our polished words.
23:7.reflection: Is my inner life with God consistent with the welcome I show on the outside?
23:7.action: Choose one area today where your words and your heart don't match, and honestly tell God about it.
23:7.prayer: Search me, Lord, and know my heart. Where my words are warm but my heart is cold, change me. Make me sincere in generosity, honest in love, and whole before You. In Jesus' name, amen.

23:8.devotion: Continuing the picture of the grudging host, this verse warns that hospitality given unwillingly brings no blessing. The guest's enjoyment turns sour, and kind words spoken over a resentful table accomplish nothing. Forced warmth and reluctant sharing leave everyone emptier than before.
23:8.reflection: When have I given something while resenting it, and what did it do to the giver and receiver?
23:8.action: If you agree to help someone today, give gladly—or kindly decline rather than give with a grudging heart.
23:8.prayer: Father, teach me to give cheerfully, not under compulsion. Guard me from bitter generosity that blesses no one. Purify my motives so that my sharing brings joy to others and honor to You. Amen.

23:9.devotion: This proverb advises discernment about when wisdom is worth speaking. Some listeners scorn correction, and repeated offers only invite contempt. The point is not to hide truth from anyone, but to recognize that words of wisdom need a receptive heart to bear any fruit.
23:9.reflection: Do I share correction wisely, or do I keep offering wisdom to those who have shown they scorn it?
23:9.action: Before offering advice today, pause and ask whether the person is open to hearing it; pray for the right timing.
23:9.prayer: Lord, give me discernment about when to speak and when to stay silent. Keep me from casting precious truth before scorn, and make my words timely and gracious. Teach me also to receive wisdom humbly myself. Amen.

23:10.devotion: In ancient Israel, boundary stones marked family inheritances, and moving them was a way of stealing land—especially from widows and orphans who had no defender. God's law protected the vulnerable, and this proverb warns against exploiting those who cannot protect their own property and futures.
23:10.reflection: Where might I be tempted to take advantage of someone who has little power to resist?
23:10.action: Look for one person with little influence or voice today, and treat their interests as carefully as your own.
23:10.prayer: Mighty God, You defend the fatherless and the widow. Keep me from ever profiting at the expense of the vulnerable. Give me integrity in business, honesty in dealings, and compassion for those the world overlooks. Amen.

23:11.devotion: This verse gives the reason for the warning: the fatherless have a mighty Redeemer. In Israel's law, a kinsman-redeemer defended family members who could not defend themselves. God Himself takes up that role, pleading the cause of the exploited against whoever wrongs them.
23:11.reflection: Do I live as though God truly defends the vulnerable—and does my treatment of them reflect that?
23:11.action: Support one ministry or act of practical help today that serves children, widows, or others without advocates.
23:11.prayer: Redeemer God, thank You that You plead the cause of those who have no voice. Make me an ally of the defenseless, never their oppressor. Use my hands and words to stand with those You defend. Amen.

23:12.devotion: Turning from warnings to the student, this verse calls for intentional, wholehearted learning. Instruction and knowledge are not absorbed passively; they require a heart applied to them and ears tuned to receive. Wisdom grows in those who deliberately make room for teaching.
23:12.reflection: Am I actively pursuing instruction, or has my teachability grown dull?
23:12.action: Set aside fifteen minutes today to study Scripture or another source of godly instruction without distraction.
23:12.prayer: Father, give me a heart that applies itself to instruction and ears that welcome knowledge. Keep me humble and teachable all my life. Let Your Word shape my thinking, my choices, and my character day by day. In Jesus' name, amen.

23:13.devotion: In ancient wisdom culture, the rod was the ordinary image for parental discipline, and this proverb urges parents not to neglect correction altogether. The core principle is that loving, timely discipline shapes a child toward life. Today, Christians apply this through consistent, gentle correction rather than reading it as an endorsement of physical punishment.
23:13.reflection: Do I correct the children and learners in my care with patience, or do I avoid the hard work of guidance?
23:13.action: If a child in your life needs correction today, do it calmly, consistently, and with clear affection afterward.
23:13.prayer: Lord, give parents and mentors wisdom to discipline in love—firm, patient, and kind. Protect children from harshness, and let every correction point them toward You. Make our homes places of both truth and tenderness. Amen.

23:14.devotion: This verse completes the thought: discipline, rightly given, delivers a child from destructive paths. The imagery of the rod belongs to its ancient setting; the enduring truth is that children need loving boundaries to turn from folly toward life. Correction is an act of hope, not anger.
23:14.reflection: Do the boundaries I set for those I love express hope for their future, or merely my frustration in the moment?
23:14.action: Review one boundary you set for a child or learner this week, and adjust it in fairness and love if needed.
23:14.prayer: Father, help me see discipline as an investment in someone's future, not an outlet for my temper. Give me steady, loving consistency with those in my care, and guard the children I love on paths of life. Amen.

23:15.devotion: A father speaks tenderly to his son, expressing how deeply his own heart is tied to the child's wellbeing. In the book of Proverbs, wisdom is not merely a set of rules but a matter of the heart. The father says that true joy for a parent comes from seeing a child choose wisdom from the inside out.
23:15.reflection: Who in my life rejoices when my heart grows wiser, and how can I honor that relationship today?
23:15.action: Reach out today to someone who has invested in your spiritual growth and thank them for their care.
23:15.prayer: Lord, make my heart wise in Your ways. May those who love and pray for me see fruit in my life that brings them joy, and may my choices honor You. Amen.

23:16.devotion: The father continues his heartfelt plea, imagining his own inmost being rejoicing when his son's words are right and true. In Proverbs, speech flows from the heart, so right words reveal inner wisdom. A parent's deepest delight is not a child's success but a child's faithful, honest speech.
23:16.reflection: Do my everyday words reflect a heart that is being shaped by God's wisdom?
23:16.action: Choose one conversation today where you will speak with extra honesty, kindness, and self-control.
23:16.prayer: Father, guard my tongue today. Let my words be right and true, bringing encouragement to others and joy to those who love me. May my speech flow from a heart aligned with You. Amen.

23:17.devotion: This verse warns against envying people who ignore God, whose lives may look easy or successful for a time. Instead, the writer calls for steady zeal for the fear of the LORD, a reverent trust that lasts all day long. Envy drains the soul; reverence for God steadies it.
23:17.reflection: When I compare my life to others who seem to prosper without God, what feelings rise up in me?
23:17.action: Notice one moment of envy today and replace it with a brief prayer of gratitude for God's presence in your life.
23:17.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times I envy others. Keep my heart anchored in reverence for You all day long, trusting that walking with You is worth more than anything I lack. Amen.

23:18.devotion: Here the father gives the reason behind his warning against envy: there is a hereafter, a future beyond the present moment. For those who fear the LORD, hope is not cut off. What looks like gain for the godless may be temporary, but God's promise to the faithful endures.
23:18.reflection: How does remembering that my story extends beyond today change what I envy and what I pursue?
23:18.action: Write down one hope you hold in God and place it somewhere visible to encourage you this week.
23:18.prayer: Father, thank You that my hope in You will not be cut off. When the success of others tempts me to envy, fix my eyes on the future You have promised. Strengthen my trust today. Amen.

23:19.devotion: The father urges his son to listen and be wise, and then gives a striking instruction: guide your heart in the way. Scripture treats the heart not as something we must simply follow, but as something we can direct, train, and lead toward God's path by deliberate, daily choices.
23:19.reflection: In what direction am I currently guiding my heart, and does that direction match the way of wisdom?
23:19.action: Identify one habit, influence, or routine that is steering your heart away from God, and take one step today to change it.
23:19.prayer: Lord, my heart can drift without Your help. Teach me to guide it deliberately along Your way. Give me wisdom to hear instruction and courage to make choices that lead me closer to You. Amen.

23:20.devotion: Practical wisdom follows: the father warns his son not to keep company with heavy drinkers and gluttons. In Proverbs, companions shape character, and repeated indulgence dulls judgment. This is not a call to despise struggling people, but a realistic warning about the habits and crowds that slowly pull a life off course.
23:20.reflection: Which relationships or routines in my life are quietly shaping my appetites and habits in the wrong direction?
23:20.action: Review your plans this week and limit time spent in settings that consistently feed unhealthy habits, choosing one better alternative instead.
23:20.prayer: Father, give me discernment about the company I keep and the habits I form. Help me choose friendships and routines that strengthen me, and grant compassion and wisdom toward those caught in struggle. Amen.

23:21.devotion: The warning continues with the consequences of unchecked indulgence: the drunkard and the glutton come to poverty, and drowsiness, laziness, clothes a person in rags. This is a general observation about how dissipation and sloth erode a life over time, not a claim that every poor person is at fault for poverty.
23:21.reflection: Are there appetites or habits of indulgence in my life that, if left unchecked, could cost me more than they give?
23:21.action: Choose one area of excess, food, spending, or leisure, and set a simple, specific boundary for today.
23:21.prayer: Lord, help me live with self-control and steady diligence. Where indulgence or laziness has crept into my life, awaken me by Your Spirit and teach me habits that honor You and bless others. Amen.

23:22.devotion: The father grounds wisdom in family honor: listen to the father who brought you into being, and do not despise your mother when she is old. Aging parents can be overlooked, but Scripture calls for lifelong respect and attentive care. Honoring parents is a mark of wisdom that continues far beyond childhood.
23:22.reflection: How am I treating my parents, or the older people God has placed in my life, especially as they age?
23:22.action: Call or visit a parent or an elderly person today; listen patiently and offer one practical act of help.
23:22.prayer: Father, thank You for the gift of parents and elders. Forgive me for impatience or neglect. Teach me to listen with respect and care for those growing old, honoring You through my love for them. Amen.

23:23.devotion: In a passage urging a son to heed wise instruction, this proverb treats truth as treasure worth every cost. Truth, wisdom, instruction, and understanding are pictured as possessions to be acquired eagerly and never traded away, no matter what the world offers in exchange.
23:23.reflection: What have I been tempted to trade for convenience or comfort lately?
23:23.action: Choose one truth of Scripture today and act on it, even when an easier, less honest option appears.
23:23.prayer: Father, make me a person who treasures Your truth above profit, popularity, or ease. Guard me from selling what is precious for what is temporary, and root my choices in Your wisdom today. Amen.

23:24.devotion: Wisdom's rewards extend beyond the individual to the whole household. This verse paints a father's deep joy at seeing his child walk in righteousness. In Proverbs' wisdom culture, a child who embraces godly instruction brings lasting delight to parents who raised them in it.
23:24.reflection: Whose joy might my choices bring, and whose heart might they grieve?
23:24.action: Thank a parent, mentor, or spiritual elder today for the wisdom they invested in you.
23:24.prayer: Lord, I want my life to bring gladness to those who have loved and guided me. Help me walk in righteousness so that my family and mentors rejoice, and let me honor their faithful investment. Amen.

23:25.devotion: Following the promise of a rejoicing father, this verse becomes a personal plea: let your parents be glad. In Proverbs, honoring father and mother is not merely duty but a source of genuine joy for them, especially when a son or daughter embraces wisdom and righteousness.
23:25.reflection: Does my way of living make my parents' hearts glad or heavy?
23:25.action: Reach out to your parents, or someone who played that role, with words of gratitude or an update that brings them joy.
23:25.prayer: Heavenly Father, help me honor those who bore and raised me, not only in words but in a wise and faithful life. Let them rejoice because of who I am becoming through Your grace. Amen.

23:26.devotion: Here the father-teacher moves from external rules to the heart itself: give me your heart. Biblical wisdom is never mere behavior management; God desires wholehearted devotion. Observing the teacher's ways follows naturally when the heart has first been surrendered and the affections directed rightly.
23:26.reflection: Is my heart fully given to God, or only my outward compliance?
23:26.action: Identify one area where your heart resists God today, and consciously surrender it to Him in a moment of prayer.
23:26.prayer: Father, I give You my heart today—my loves, my loyalties, my desires. Let my eyes watch Your ways and my steps follow them, so that my whole life flows from a heart devoted to You. Amen.

23:27.devotion: Continuing his warning against sexual temptation, the father uses vivid imagery: a deep pit and a narrow well. Both pictures suggest danger that is easy to fall into and hard to escape. The verse warns of consequences that entangle, not to shame victims of exploitation but to urge the young toward forethought and self-control.
23:27.reflection: What tempting path am I treating as harmless, though it leads somewhere hard to escape?
23:27.action: Name one risky situation you keep drifting toward, and take one practical step today to set a boundary around it.
23:27.prayer: Lord, give me clear eyes to see where a path leads before I walk it. Guard my heart and body from choices that entangle, and grant me the strength to turn away while turning is still easy. Amen.

23:28.devotion: The warning deepens: seduction does not merely happen; it lies in wait. Proverbs personifies folly as actively hunting the unwary, multiplying unfaithfulness among many. The instruction calls readers to vigilance, recognizing that temptation often ambushes those who assume they are standing safely out of reach.
23:28.reflection: Where am I most likely to be caught off guard by temptation?
23:28.action: Ask a trusted friend to pray with you about one specific area of vulnerability, and check in with them regularly.
23:28.prayer: Father, keep me alert to the traps I cannot see from where I stand. Surround me with honest companions, steady my heart when temptation waits in ambush, and keep me faithful to You and to others. Amen.

23:29.devotion: With a series of piercing rhetorical questions, the father sketches a portrait of a ruined life: woe, sorrow, strife, complaints, needless wounds, and bloodshot eyes. This vivid description builds toward its answer in the next verse, inviting the listener to recognize misery's recognizable face and ask what produces it.
23:29.reflection: What patterns in my life are quietly producing sorrow rather than joy?
23:29.action: Honestly review your week and name one habit causing you or others grief; write it down and bring it to God in prayer.
23:29.prayer: Lord, open my eyes to where sorrow is entering my life. Give me honesty to name it, courage to change it, and compassion for others caught in struggles I do not fully understand. Lead me in Your peace. Amen.

23:30.devotion: The questions of the previous verse find their answer here: those who linger long over wine and hunt after mixed drinks. Proverbs warns against excess and addiction, not to condemn those struggling with dependence but to urge restraint before harm begins. Lingering is the problem; the pursuit of intoxication breeds the sorrows just described.
23:30.reflection: Is there anything I linger over too long, letting it control me rather than serving it?
23:30.action: Set one concrete limit today on a habit you know tends to run past healthy boundaries, and keep it.
23:30.prayer: Father, grant me self-control and honesty about my habits. Where anything has mastery over me, break its grip by Your grace, and help me walk in freedom and sober-mindedness, caring for my body as Your temple. Amen.

23:31.devotion: This proverb warns against being captivated by the allure of intoxicating wine. The vivid imagery of sparkling, swirling drink captures how temptation presents itself as beautiful and desirable. The wisdom writer urges us not even to linger looking at what draws us toward harm, teaching that resisting temptation often begins with where we fix our attention.
23:31.reflection: What alluring thing in my life deserves less of my gaze and attention?
23:31.action: Identify one temptation you habitually linger over, and take a practical step today to remove or reduce your exposure to it.
23:31.prayer: Father, guard my eyes and my heart. Help me look away from what sparkles but harms, and turn my attention toward what is good, pure, and life-giving. Give me strength to choose wisely today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

23:32.devotion: Following the warning about wine's appeal, this verse reveals its hidden cost. What seems pleasant in the moment ultimately bites like a serpent. Scripture here teaches sober honesty about consequences: sin and excess often promise delight but deliver pain, and wisdom weighs the end of a thing before embracing its beginning.
23:32.reflection: Am I honest with myself about where this pleasure actually leads?
23:32.action: Write down one habit you're tempted by, then list its real long-term costs. Review that list whenever temptation feels attractive.
23:32.prayer: Lord, give me clear eyes to see past the moment's pleasure to its true end. Save me from choices that promise sweetness but sting. Anchor me in wisdom that considers consequences before acting. Amen.

23:33.devotion: This verse describes the tragic effects of drunkenness: impaired perception and corrupted speech. Under wine's influence, a person sees what is not real and speaks what should never be said. The passage reminds us that losing self-control exposes us to deception and dishonors the God who calls our words and witness to reflect Him.
23:33.reflection: Have I ever said or believed things under influence that I later regretted?
23:33.action: Practice self-control in one area today, whether speech, media, or consumption, and notice how clear your mind and words remain.
23:33.prayer: Father, keep my mind clear and my tongue faithful. Protect me from anything that distorts my perception or corrupts my speech. Let my words honor You and reflect a heart governed by Your Spirit. Amen.

23:34.devotion: The proverb pictures drunkenness as lying in the sea or atop a swaying mast, unstable, disoriented, and unsafe. Wine strips a person of stability and good judgment. The image teaches that whatever robs us of self-control leaves us vulnerable, and wisdom calls us to remain grounded and steady in clear-minded dependence on God.
23:34.reflection: Where in my life am I spiritually unsteady because of a compromised habit?
23:34.action: Choose one grounding rhythm today, such as prayer, Scripture reading, or a walk, and keep it even if life feels busy.
23:34.prayer: Lord, be my stability. Keep me steady when circumstances sway and temptation clouds my judgment. Ground me in Your truth so that I stand firm, clear-eyed and secure, in every situation today. Amen.

23:35.devotion: This verse ends the drinking passage with sobering irony: the drunk person feels beaten yet numb, then wakes hoping to seek another drink. It exposes the repetitive grip of excess, how it dulls pain while deepening bondage. The wisdom writer shows that some comforts do not heal us but quietly teach us to crave them more.
23:35.reflection: Am I returning to something for comfort that only deepens my need?
23:35.action: If a habit has a repeated grip on you, share it honestly with a trusted friend or mentor today and ask for prayer and accountability.
23:35.prayer: Father, expose any cycle in my life that numbs pain but deepens bondage. Give me courage to face what I've avoided and freedom in Your strength. Surround me with people who will help me walk in truth. Amen.

24:1.devotion: The wisdom writer turns from excess to envy, warning against desiring the lives of evil people or wanting their company. Their apparent success can make wrongdoing look attractive. Scripture calls us to measure people not by outcomes but by character, and to find our longing satisfied in God rather than in what the wicked seem to enjoy.
24:1.reflection: Whose success am I quietly envying, and is their character worth imitating?
24:1.action: Name one person you've envied, then thank God today for three good gifts He has already placed in your own life.
24:1.prayer: Lord, forgive me for envying those who prosper by wrong. Free my heart from comparison. Teach me to delight in Your ways and trust that walking with You is worth more than any gain gained unjustly. Amen.

24:2.devotion: This verse explains why envy of the wicked is dangerous: their hearts devise violence and their lips stir up trouble. Who we draw near to shapes us. The proverb is not about despising sinners, whom Jesus came to seek, but about not joining ourselves to people whose plans and words are given over to harm.
24:2.reflection: Are the people closest to me pushing me toward wisdom or trouble?
24:2.action: Evaluate your closest influences today. If one relationship consistently pulls you toward harmful choices, plan a wise boundary for this week.
24:2.prayer: Father, grant me discernment about the voices I welcome close. Keep me from companionship that fuels trouble, and surround me with people whose hearts and words honor You. Make me an influence for good in return. Amen.

24:3.devotion: Here the proverbs turn toward hope: wisdom builds a house and understanding establishes it. A household, life, or endeavor grows stable not through shortcuts or schemes but through godly wisdom patiently applied. This verse invites us to value the slow, steady work of understanding, trusting that what God's wisdom builds will stand.
24:3.reflection: What am I building right now, and is wisdom holding the tools?
24:3.action: Choose one area of your life, home, work, or faith, and take one deliberate step today to build it with prayerful wisdom rather than hurry.
24:3.prayer: Lord, I want to build what lasts. Fill me with Your wisdom and establish my life by Your understanding. Teach me to value steady, godly work over shortcuts, and let everything I build honor You. Amen.

24:4.devotion: In this proverb, a house being built through wisdom pictures a life well-ordered. Knowledge fills its rooms with riches that are precious and pleasant. The passage values growth in understanding as the true source of an abundant, hospitable life rather than wealth gained hastily.
24:4.reflection: What am I doing to fill the rooms of my life with knowledge rather than mere possessions?
24:4.action: Set aside twenty minutes today to learn something valuable—read Scripture, a good book, or study a skill that serves others.
24:4.prayer: Lord, fill every room of my life with Your wisdom. Make my inner house a place of pleasant riches—understanding, kindness, and truth—that others may be blessed when they enter. Amen.

24:5.devotion: Wisdom is pictured here as a form of strength. A wise man is strong because understanding equips him for challenges that raw power cannot handle. Knowledge increases strength over time, as learned discernment steadies a person where physical might alone would fail.
24:5.reflection: Where am I relying on effort alone when God offers me strength through wisdom?
24:5.action: Before your next difficult decision, pause and ask one knowledgeable, godly person for their perspective.
24:5.prayer: Father, I confess I often trust my own effort more than Your wisdom. Grow me in knowledge and understanding, that my strength would rest in You and not in myself alone. Amen.

24:6.devotion: Ancient kings prepared for battle with gathered counsel, and this proverb applies that principle to everyday life: wise counsel leads to victory, and many counselors bring safety. It encourages humility—we make better decisions when we refuse to rely only on our own judgment.
24:6.reflection: When was the last time I genuinely sought advice instead of trusting only my own instincts?
24:6.action: Identify one decision you are facing and schedule a conversation this week with two trusted, mature counselors.
24:6.prayer: Lord, forgive my prideful independence. Surround me with wise and honest voices, and give me humility to listen. Guard my steps through the counsel You provide, and lead me in safety. Amen.

24:7.devotion: The city gate was where legal matters and public decisions were settled. A fool, lacking wisdom, has nothing worthwhile to contribute there. The proverb warns that wisdom must be pursued and received, or a person becomes unfit for meaningful responsibility and influence in the community.
24:7.reflection: Am I pursuing wisdom so I can contribute well, or am I neglecting it and falling behind?
24:7.action: Choose one area where you feel unprepared, and take one step today toward learning and growing in it.
24:7.prayer: Father, keep me from being a fool who has nothing to offer when it matters. Open my heart to Your wisdom now, so I may serve others faithfully when I am needed. Amen.

24:8.devotion: This proverb exposes the person who quietly plans harm; such scheming earns a reputation. The point is simple: our secret plans shape our public character. Someone who devises evil eventually becomes known for it, no matter how carefully the plotting is hidden at first.
24:8.reflection: What do my private plans and daydreams reveal about the person I am becoming?
24:8.action: Examine your motives in one current plan or project, and if any part serves selfish harm, confess it and correct it today.
24:8.prayer: Search me, O God, and know my thoughts. Expose any hidden scheming in my heart, and replace it with honest, generous intentions that honor You and bless the people around me. Amen.

24:9.devotion: Here wisdom teaching names foolishness plainly: devising evil is sin, and the scoffer who mocks what is good becomes repulsive to others. The verse calls us to take seriously not only our actions but the attitudes and plans that flow from a foolish or contemptuous heart.
24:9.reflection: Do I treat sarcastic scoffing and careless plotting as harmless, when God calls them sin?
24:9.action: Catch yourself once today before you scoff or joke at someone's expense, and choose an encouraging word instead.
24:9.prayer: Lord, purify not only my deeds but my thoughts and my tongue. Deliver me from scoffing and foolish scheming, and let my words and plans be clean, kind, and pleasing to You. Amen.

24:10.devotion: This proverb offers a sober test of character: adversity reveals how much strength we truly have. Fainting in a difficult day exposes small reserves. The wisdom teaching urges us to build endurance beforehand, so that when trouble comes we do not collapse but stand firm by God's help.
24:10.reflection: How do I respond when adversity strikes—do I persevere or quietly give up on what is right?
24:10.action: Name one difficult task you have been avoiding, and take a single faithful step toward it today rather than fainting.
24:10.prayer: Father, strengthen me for the day of adversity. When pressure comes, keep me from fainting or abandoning what is right. Build in me endurance rooted in Your faithfulness and presence. Amen.

24:11.devotion: This verse moves wisdom from personal character to active rescue: those who know God must not stand by while others are dragged toward death. It commands delivering the endangered and holding back those stumbling toward harm, making protection of vulnerable lives a duty of wisdom, not an optional kindness.
24:11.reflection: Who around me is in danger or distress, and am I looking away when God calls me to act?
24:11.action: Choose one concrete way today to help someone at risk or in crisis—offer assistance, speak up for them, or connect them with help.
24:11.prayer: Lord, open my eyes to those stumbling toward harm. Give me courage not to look away but to intervene wisely and compassionately, protecting life as You call me to do. Amen.

24:12.devotion: This proverb warns against claiming ignorance to excuse our silence toward those in danger of harm. God, who weighs hearts and keeps our souls, sees whether we truly knew or chose not to know. He holds each person accountable, rendering to everyone according to what they have actually done.
24:12.reflection: Where might I be using 'I didn't know' to excuse myself from helping someone I could have helped?
24:12.action: Identify one person in need you have been overlooking, and take one practical step today to help them.
24:12.prayer: Lord, You weigh my heart and know what I truly know. Deliver me from comfortable excuses. Open my eyes to those who need rescue and give me courage to act, not look away. Amen.

24:13.devotion: In context, this earthly picture of honey's sweetness and goodness sets up the next verse's comparison. The father in Proverbs often uses simple, tangible pleasures to teach his son. Good gifts in creation, enjoyed rightly, become illustrations of deeper spiritual realities worth desiring and receiving.
24:13.reflection: What simple good pleasure in my life can remind me today to hunger for wisdom in the same way?
24:13.action: Enjoy one of God's simple gifts today, and let it prompt a moment of gratitude and a pause to seek His wisdom.
24:13.prayer: Father, thank You for good and sweet things in Your creation. Teach me through them to desire what is truly nourishing. Give me a taste for wisdom that makes me hunger for it daily. Amen.

24:14.devotion: The sweetness of honey becomes a picture of wisdom for the soul. Just as honey delights the taste, wisdom brings inward delight and a sure expectation for the future. The proverb promises that those who find wisdom have a genuine prospect ahead, and their hope will not be cut off.
24:14.reflection: Do I treasure wisdom as something sweet to be sought, or treat it as a burden to be tolerated?
24:14.action: Set aside fifteen minutes today to read Scripture specifically seeking wisdom, and note one insight to apply.
24:14.prayer: Lord, make wisdom sweet to my soul. Help me seek it like something delicious and precious, and anchor my hope in what You promise, so that my expectations rest firmly in You. Amen.

24:15.devotion: This verse addresses the wicked directly, warning against scheming to plunder the home and resting place of the righteous. It names this exploitation for what it is, describing a real temptation in an unjust world without blaming the righteous for being targeted. It stands as a warning to would-be oppressors.
24:15.reflection: Am I ever tempted to gain advantage by taking what belongs to someone more vulnerable than I am?
24:15.action: Examine one area of work or finances today where you hold power, and ensure you are treating the other party fairly.
24:15.prayer: Father, keep me from any scheme that harms others for my gain. Guard my heart from greed and from exploiting the vulnerable. Make me someone who protects the rest and security of others. Amen.

24:16.devotion: This proverb contrasts the righteous and the wicked by their different responses to downfall. The righteous person may fall repeatedly, even seven times in the Bible's symbolic fullness, yet rises again through repentance and God's grace. The wicked, by contrast, stumble into calamity without recovery when disaster finally overtakes them.
24:16.reflection: When I fall into failure or sin, do I get back up with God's help, or do I stay down in discouragement?
24:16.action: Name one recent failure honestly before God today, receive His forgiveness, and take one step to rise again.
24:16.prayer: Gracious Father, thank You that falling is not the end for those who belong to You. When I stumble, lift me up by Your mercy and strengthen me to rise again and walk with You. Amen.

24:17.devotion: This proverb restrains a surprising but common temptation: secret gladness when an enemy falls. God's people are called to a higher posture than spite. Their enemy's stumble is not cause for celebration, and the following verse shows the Lord sees such rejoicing and is displeased by it.
24:17.reflection: When someone who has wronged me suffers, what honestly rises in my heart, and do I let it stay there?
24:17.action: Think of one person you resent, and pray a genuine blessing over them today instead of savoring any grudge.
24:17.prayer: Lord, search my heart and cleanse it of hidden gloating and spite. Give me Your compassion even toward those who have hurt me, and let my heart respond to others' troubles with mercy. Amen.

24:18.devotion: This verse explains the previous warning: the Lord sees the secret rejoicing over an enemy's downfall, and it displeases Him. The consequence described is sobering: He may turn His wrath away from that enemy. God governs even our attitudes toward our adversaries and takes our spite seriously.
24:18.reflection: Do I remember that the Lord sees not only my enemy's failings, but also my private reactions to them?
24:18.action: When you catch yourself enjoying someone's misfortune today, pause, confess it to God, and ask Him to soften your heart.
24:18.prayer: Father, You see every corner of my heart, even my thoughts about my enemies. Forgive my secret satisfaction when others fall, and shape in me a mercy that reflects Your own patient heart. Amen.

24:19.devotion: This proverb addresses the frustration of watching evildoers prosper. The command is doubled: do not fret, and do not envy. Anxiety over injustice and desire for the wicked's success both corrode the heart. God's people are called to a steadier trust rather than turmoil over those who seem to thrive.
24:19.reflection: When I see unjust people succeeding, does fretting and envy quietly take root in my heart?
24:19.action: Write down one situation where you envy or resent someone's success, and release it to God in a written prayer today.
24:19.prayer: Lord, when evildoers seem to prosper, quiet my fretting and uproot my envy. Anchor my peace in You and Your justice, and keep my heart from turmoil over what I cannot control. Amen.

24:20.devotion: This proverb warns that a life built on evil has no lasting future. The image of a lamp put out speaks of hope, prosperity, and legacy coming to an end. The wise person chooses the steady, enduring path of righteousness rather than the fleeting gains of wickedness.
24:20.reflection: Where am I tempted to seek short-term gain in ways that compromise my integrity before God?
24:20.action: Identify one area today where you are tempted to cut corners ethically, and choose the honest path instead.
24:20.prayer: Father, keep my eyes on what endures. Turn me from any path that promises quick reward but leads away from You. Let my hope rest in righteousness, and light my way with Your truth. Amen.

24:21.devotion: A father counsels his son to honor both God and lawful authority, and to avoid restless people constantly agitating for upheaval. The verse calls for a settled reverence toward the Lord that shapes how we relate to order and community rather than joining every cause of discontent.
24:21.reflection: Do I practice genuine reverence for God and respect for rightful authority, or am I drawn toward constant agitation?
24:21.action: Pray for wisdom today about one situation where you feel discontent, seeking a constructive response rather than restless complaint.
24:21.prayer: Lord, teach me to fear You above all and to honor the authorities You have placed over me. Guard me from a restless, unsettled spirit, and anchor my heart in Your steady wisdom and peace. Amen.

24:22.devotion: Continuing the father's warning, this verse explains why we should avoid those given to rebellion: their collapse can come suddenly and without warning. The ruin they bring can be widespread. Wisdom values stability and discernment over being swept into turmoil by others' instability.
24:22.reflection: Am I discerning about whose influence I allow into my life, or do I follow crowds without weighing the consequences?
24:22.action: Consider one relationship or group that pulls you toward turmoil, and set a wise boundary there today.
24:22.prayer: Father, give me discernment about the influences around me. Save me from being swept into trouble by others' choices, and make my steps firm in Your wisdom, so my life brings stability rather than ruin. Amen.

24:23.devotion: This saying belongs to the collection of words of the wise. It declares that showing partiality in judgment—favoring some people over others because of status, wealth, or connection—is not good. Justice requires treating every person fairly, reflecting God's own impartial and righteous character.
24:23.reflection: Do I judge people fairly, or do I quietly favor those I like, know, or benefit from?
24:23.action: Notice one decision today where you might favor someone unfairly, and deliberately treat everyone involved by the same standard.
24:23.prayer: Righteous God, You judge with perfect fairness. Expose any partiality in my heart, and teach me to treat every person with the same honesty and dignity, reflecting Your just character in my daily decisions. Amen.

24:24.devotion: This proverb warns against calling wickedness righteous. When leaders or judges excuse evil and praise the guilty, they lose the trust of the people and bring dishonor on themselves and their communities. Truth-telling protects a society; flattering evil corrodes it and invites deserved contempt.
24:24.reflection: Am I ever tempted to affirm wrong behavior because speaking truth would cost me something?
24:24.action: Choose one situation today where honesty about right and wrong is needed, and speak the truth graciously.
24:24.prayer: Lord, keep me from calling evil good to win approval or avoid conflict. Give me courage to name wrongdoing honestly and kindly, and let my words serve truth even when flattery would be easier. Amen.

24:25.devotion: In contrast to the one who excuses wickedness, this proverb promises that those who confront evil will find delight, and a good blessing will come upon them. Honest rebuke is hard, but it brings a clear conscience, God's favor, and the deep satisfaction of standing for what is right.
24:25.reflection: Do I see truthful confrontation as a burden to avoid, or as an act that brings blessing?
24:25.action: If you have been avoiding a needed, honest conversation, take one step toward having it kindly today.
24:25.prayer: Father, thank You that truth-telling, though difficult, carries Your blessing. Strengthen me to speak honestly when wrongdoing needs to be addressed, and let the delight of a clear conscience draw me closer to You. Amen.

24:26.devotion: An honest, right answer is compared to a kiss—a sign of warm affection and honor. Truthful words, spoken at the right moment, are a gift of love. When we answer plainly and justly, we honor the listener and build relationships on trust rather than flattery or evasion.
24:26.reflection: Are my answers to others honest and timely, or do I dodge, flatter, and delay the truth?
24:26.action: Give one straightforward, honest answer today to a question you might normally sidestep, doing so kindly.
24:26.prayer: Lord, make my words trustworthy. Help me answer others honestly and graciously, so that my speech becomes an act of love and honor rather than evasion. Let truth and kindness shape everything I say today. Amen.

24:27.devotion: This proverb counsels practical order: establish your livelihood and work in the field first, then build your house. Wisdom plans ahead, providing a stable foundation before taking on larger commitments. Diligent preparation and right priorities protect a household from needless hardship and strain.
24:27.reflection: Am I building my life on stable foundations, or rushing into commitments before the groundwork is laid?
24:27.action: Choose one project or goal and list the foundational steps you should complete first, then start one today.
24:27.prayer: Father, You honor wise planning and patient work. Help me order my priorities well, laying steady foundations before taking on more. Teach me diligence and patience in the ordinary tasks that sustain the life You've given me. Amen.

24:28.devotion: This proverb warns against giving testimony against a neighbor when there is no genuine reason. Words spoken carelessly or dishonestly can wound reputations and relationships. God calls His people to truthful speech that protects others rather than deceives, using our lips to build up, not to tear down.
24:28.reflection: Have I spoken about someone in a way that exaggerated, assumed, or distorted the truth?
24:28.action: Before discussing anyone today, pause and ask whether your words are truthful, necessary, and fair.
24:28.prayer: Lord, guard my lips today. Keep me from careless or dishonest words about others. Help me speak truth in love and protect my neighbor's good name as I would want mine protected. In Jesus' name, amen.

24:29.devotion: Wisdom forbids personal retaliation. When we are wronged, the natural impulse is to pay back injury for injury, but Scripture calls us to leave justice with God and respond with grace. Rejecting revenge frees our hearts from bitterness and reflects the mercy we ourselves have received.
24:29.reflection: Am I holding onto a desire to get even with someone who has hurt me?
24:29.action: Choose one grudge you carry and, today, take a step toward releasing it, perhaps through prayer or a kind act toward that person.
24:29.prayer: Father, when I am wronged, remind me that revenge belongs to You, not me. Soften my heart, uproot bitterness, and give me grace to forgive as You have forgiven me. In Jesus' name, amen.

24:30.devotion: The writer describes passing by a neglected field and vineyard belonging to someone lacking sense. This begins a vivid object lesson drawn from everyday life: an unkempt property tells a story about neglected responsibility. Wisdom often teaches through simple observations of the world around us.
24:30.reflection: What neglected area of my life, if I passed by it honestly, would look like this overgrown field?
24:30.action: Identify one responsibility you have been putting off and spend fifteen minutes today making a start on it.
24:30.prayer: Lord, open my eyes to the places in my life I have allowed to go untended. Give me honesty to see them and diligence to begin restoring what neglect has allowed to fall into disrepair. Amen.

24:31.devotion: The neglected field is covered with thorns and nettles, its protective wall broken down. Neglect does not leave things as they are; it allows ruin to creep in slowly. The image shows how small omissions, over time, allow destruction that careful attention would have prevented.
24:31.reflection: What small daily neglects in my life are quietly allowing thorns to grow?
24:31.action: Notice one small habit of neglect today, such as skipped prayer or unfinished tasks, and correct it before the day ends.
24:31.prayer: Father, thank You for teaching me through simple pictures. Show me where small neglects are taking root, and help me tend faithfully what You have placed in my care, one small act at a time. Amen.

24:32.devotion: The writer does not merely glance at the ruined field; he considers it well and receives instruction. Wisdom requires reflection, not just observation. God can teach us through what we see if we slow down, ponder it, and let the lesson shape how we live.
24:32.reflection: Do I take time to reflect on what life's ordinary scenes are teaching me?
24:32.action: Set aside ten quiet minutes today to reflect on a recent experience and write down one lesson it holds for you.
24:32.prayer: Lord, slow me down enough to truly see and consider. Teach me through the ordinary moments of my day, and let reflection lead to wisdom and change rather than passing by unchanged. Amen.

24:33.devotion: The lesson of the field is summarized: a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands. Ruin rarely arrives through one dramatic failure; it comes through small, repeated choices. The proverb warns that drifting into laziness happens little by little, almost unnoticed.
24:33.reflection: What 'little' compromise or postponement am I repeating that could gradually become a serious problem?
24:33.action: Name one recurring small delay in your day, and replace it today with a single faithful step of diligence.
24:33.prayer: Father, keep me alert to the small choices that shape my character. Deliver me from slow drift and complacency, and give me steady faithfulness in the little things that matter to You. Amen.

24:34.devotion: The proverb concludes with a sober image: poverty comes like a prowler and need like an armed man. Neglect's consequences arrive suddenly and forcefully, even though they grew from small, slow habits. The warning is meant to stir diligence now, before scarcity makes its unwelcome entrance.
24:34.reflection: If my current habits continue unchanged, where might they lead me in a few years?
24:34.action: Choose one area, such as finances, health, or relationships, and take one deliberate preventive step today rather than waiting for trouble.
24:34.prayer: Lord, give me the wisdom to see where my habits are heading before consequences arrive. Help me act today with diligence and foresight, trusting You as I steward what You have entrusted to me. Amen.

25:1.devotion: This verse introduces a new section: proverbs of Solomon copied by men serving King Hezekiah of Judah, roughly two centuries after Solomon's reign. It reminds us that God's wisdom was carefully preserved and passed down through faithful hands, so later generations could continue learning from it.
25:1.reflection: Am I faithfully passing on the wisdom God has taught me to those who come after me?
25:1.action: Share one piece of biblical wisdom God has taught you with a friend, child, or younger believer today.
25:1.prayer: Thank You, Lord, for preserving Your wisdom through faithful people across generations. Help me treasure Your Word, live it out, and pass it on to others so that Your truth endures. In Jesus' name, amen.

25:2.devotion: This proverb begins a collection of Solomon's sayings copied by Hezekiah's scribes. It honors both divine mystery and human diligence: God's wisdom runs deeper than we can exhaust, yet He invites us to seek, study, and discover. Searching out truth is not pride but a noble calling for those who lead and serve.
25:2.reflection: Where might God be inviting you to dig deeper rather than settle for easy answers?
25:2.action: Spend fifteen minutes today studying one Bible passage carefully, using a cross-reference or commentary to go beneath the surface.
25:2.prayer: Father, thank You for mysteries worth searching out. Give me a patient, humble mind that delights in Your Word and pursues truth diligently, trusting that You reward those who earnestly seek You. Amen.

25:3.devotion: Just as no one can measure the sky's height or the earth's depth, the inner thoughts of rulers remain beyond full knowledge. The proverb counsels humility before authority: we rarely know all the considerations behind another person's decisions, so we should withhold quick judgments about motives we cannot see.
25:3.reflection: When have you judged someone's motives too quickly, only to learn later you lacked the full picture?
25:3.action: Before criticizing a leader's decision today, pause and list two factors you may not know about.
25:3.prayer: Lord, You alone see every heart. Cure me of rash judgments about motives I cannot know. Teach me to extend the patience to others that You so freely extend to me. Amen.

25:4.devotion: Silver becomes usable only when impurities are removed; the silversmith can craft jewelry from refined metal. The image prepares the next verse: what is true of metal is true of governance and of character. Removal of what corrupts makes way for beauty, usefulness, and honor.
25:4.reflection: What impurity in your own life is the Refiner asking you to let Him remove right now?
25:4.action: Name one habit that dulls your witness, and take one practical step today to cut it back.
25:4.prayer: Lord, You are the patient Silversmith. Search me, expose the dross in my heart, and have the courage to refine me until my life reflects Your beauty and is fit for Your service. Amen.

25:5.devotion: A ruler's throne stands firm not through force but through righteousness. Removing wicked influences from the king's presence allows justice to flourish. The principle still applies wherever we hold responsibility: organizations, families, and churches are stabilized when wrong is addressed rather than tolerated near the center of power.
25:5.reflection: Is there a harmful influence you have tolerated in a place of responsibility where righteousness requires action?
25:5.action: If you lead others, address one compromise honestly today instead of overlooking it for the sake of comfort.
25:5.prayer: Father, establish what is right and uproot what is wicked in every place where I hold influence. Give leaders wisdom to remove corruption, and give me courage to choose righteousness over convenience. Amen.

25:6.devotion: Solomon warns against self-promotion in the royal court. Pushing yourself forward, grabbing honors not yet given, invites embarrassment. Wisdom knows that genuine recognition comes from others, not from our own claims, and that humility positions us to receive what is rightly offered rather than seize what is not.
25:6.reflection: In what settings are you tempted to promote yourself rather than let your work quietly speak?
25:6.action: Resist one urge to boast today; instead, find a genuine way to credit someone else's contribution.
25:6.prayer: Lord, deliver me from the restless need to exalt myself. Teach me the freedom of humility, to serve faithfully without demanding notice, and to trust You with my reputation. Amen.

25:7.devotion: Completing the previous saying, this verse echoes Jesus' later teaching about taking the lowest seat at the banquet. It is far better to be invited upward than demoted publicly. Waiting for honor to be bestowed guards us from shame and reflects a heart that does not grasp for status.
25:7.reflection: Would you rather be overlooked for a while or be exposed as a self-promoter before people you respect?
25:7.action: Choose the lower place today in one practical situation, such as letting another person's preference or turn come first.
25:7.prayer: Lord Jesus, You humbled Yourself and were exalted by the Father. Free me from grasping for position. Give me the quiet confidence of one who knows my worth rests in You alone. Amen.

25:8.devotion: Solomon counsels restraint before rushing into legal conflict with a neighbor. Hasty lawsuits can end in public shame when the case turns out differently than expected. The wisdom here favors patience, careful thought, and reconciliation over impulsive escalation of disputes that words could have settled.
25:8.reflection: What current conflict are you tempted to escalate quickly rather than handle patiently and privately?
25:8.action: Before pursuing a dispute further today, pause for one day and consider whether a direct, gracious conversation could resolve it.
25:8.prayer: Father, slow me down when conflict stirs my emotions. Guard me from hasty actions I may regret, and give me wisdom to pursue peace with those around me rather than victory over them. Amen.

25:9.devotion: This proverb prescribes the path of private, honest resolution: present your grievance directly to the person involved, and resist the urge to broadcast the matter to others. Handling conflict this way protects reputations, preserves confidences, and reflects Jesus' later teaching about going privately to a brother who has wronged you.
25:9.reflection: Is there a grievance you have been sharing with others instead of addressing directly with the person involved?
25:9.action: If you have a dispute with someone, commit to speaking with them directly this week rather than discussing it with third parties.
25:9.prayer: Lord, give me courage to speak plainly and kindly with those I have conflict with. Keep my tongue from gossip, protect the reputations of others, and make me a peacemaker in Your church. Amen.

25:10.devotion: In a section of Solomon's proverbs about wise conduct, this verse warns against betraying a confidence or speaking carelessly about a dispute. Words shared rashly can come back to disgrace us. Wisdom guards the tongue, honoring others and protecting our own integrity before God and people.
25:10.reflection: Is there a confidence I've been tempted to share that isn't mine to tell?
25:10.action: Today, hold back one piece of information you were tempted to share, and instead pray quietly about the situation.
25:10.prayer: Father, guard my tongue today. Keep me from careless words and gossip that bring shame. Let my speech be trustworthy and honorable, reflecting Your wisdom. In Jesus' name, amen.

25:11.devotion: Solomon pictures the beauty of speech delivered at just the right moment and in just the right way. A fitting word is precious craftsmanship, like golden apples displayed on silver. Timing and tone matter as much as truth; wisdom knows when and how to speak.
25:11.reflection: Whom could I encourage with a well-timed word today?
25:11.action: Send a thoughtful, specific message of encouragement to someone who needs it, choosing your words with care.
25:11.prayer: Lord, teach me to speak words that are timely and kind. Help me notice when someone needs encouragement and give me the grace to offer it beautifully. Amen.

25:12.devotion: A wise rebuke, humbly received, is as valuable as fine gold jewelry. Correction is a gift, not an insult, when it comes from wisdom and lands on a willing heart. This proverb honors both the courageous rebuker and the obedient listener who grows from it.
25:12.reflection: When was the last time I received correction without becoming defensive?
25:12.action: Ask someone who knows you well for one honest piece of feedback, and simply listen without arguing.
25:12.prayer: Lord, give me a humble ear that welcomes wise correction. Thank You for the people You use to refine me. Help me receive truth with grace and act on it. Amen.

25:13.devotion: A trustworthy messenger is compared to cold snow on a harvest day—refreshing and welcome. Faithfulness in small assignments refreshes those who depend on us. Solomon values reliability: finishing what we're entrusted with brings life to others and joy to those we serve.
25:13.reflection: Do I follow through on what I promise, or do commitments quietly slip away?
25:13.action: Complete one task you've been putting off or left unfinished, today, before the day ends.
25:13.prayer: Faithful God, make me dependable in the small things You place before me. Let my reliability be refreshing to others and honoring to You. Strengthen me to finish well today. Amen.

25:14.devotion: Boasting of generosity one never delivers is like wind and clouds that promise rain but give none—disappointing and empty. Solomon warns against inflating our image. True giving needs no advertisement; God values quiet integrity over impressive claims that leave others thirsty.
25:14.reflection: Do my words about myself overstate what I actually do or give?
25:14.action: Do one genuine act of generosity today and tell no one about it except God in prayer.
25:14.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I've exaggerated or sought credit. Make my giving real and my words honest. Let me live for Your approval rather than appearances. In Jesus' name, amen.

25:15.devotion: This proverb praises patient, gentle persuasion. Long forbearance can soften even a ruler, and a calm tongue can accomplish what force never could—it breaks a bone, penetrating stubbornness deeply. Wisdom works slowly and kindly, not through irritation or pressure, to change hearts and outcomes.
25:15.reflection: Am I trying to change someone through pressure instead of patience?
25:15.action: Choose one tense relationship or negotiation today, and respond with a calm, gentle voice instead of pushing harder.
25:15.prayer: Lord, You are patient with me beyond measure. Teach me to persuade with gentleness and wait with forbearance. Let my calm words carry real weight in difficult conversations today. Amen.

25:16.devotion: Even honey, a good gift, becomes harmful in excess. Solomon teaches moderation: pleasure and blessing are meant to be enjoyed with restraint, not indulged until they sicken us. Wisdom enjoys God's good things while refusing the greed that turns sweetness into sickness.
25:16.reflection: What good thing in my life am I enjoying to excess right now?
25:16.action: Identify one indulgence—food, media, or spending—and set a clear, reasonable limit for it today.
25:16.prayer: Father, thank You for good gifts. Forgive my tendency toward excess. Give me self-control to enjoy Your blessings with gratitude and moderation, keeping my heart free from greed. Amen.

25:17.devotion: Good neighborliness needs healthy boundaries. Dropping by too often wears out even the friendliest welcome, Solomon warns, until weariness curdles into resentment. Love respects others' time, space, and rhythms. Wisdom knows that closeness is preserved by restraint, not constant presence.
25:17.reflection: Am I mindful of others' space and capacity, or only my own desire for company?
25:17.action: Before contacting or visiting someone today, consider whether the timing suits them, and honor their space.
25:17.prayer: Lord, help me love my neighbors with wisdom and consideration. Keep me from neediness that overwhelms, and teach me to respect the rhythms and boundaries of others. Amen.

25:18.devotion: This proverb warns how devastating lies can be. False testimony against a neighbor is compared to weapons of violence—a club, sword, and sharp arrow—because words can wound and destroy a person's reputation, livelihood, and safety as surely as physical force.
25:18.reflection: Have my words ever damaged someone's reputation, even in a small way?
25:18.action: Refuse to repeat or spread one piece of unverified information about someone today; if others gossip, gently change the subject.
25:18.prayer: Lord, guard my tongue today. Keep me from lies, exaggeration, and gossip that wound others. Let my speech be truthful and kind, building up my neighbors rather than harming them. In Jesus' name, amen.

25:19.devotion: In times of trouble, we naturally lean on those around us. This proverb cautions that trusting an unfaithful person brings disappointment and pain, like relying on a bad tooth or a dislocated foot—things that fail precisely when we need them most.
25:19.reflection: Who have I trusted with my troubles, and have they proven faithful?
25:19.action: Identify one trustworthy person in your life and thank them today for their reliability.
25:19.prayer: Father, thank You for faithful friends who stand firm in hard times. Help me be trustworthy to others, and give me wisdom to discern who is reliable. You alone never fail me. Amen.

25:20.devotion: This proverb teaches sensitivity to those who grieve. Singing cheerful songs to a heavy heart is as thoughtless as stripping someone's coat in cold weather or mixing vinegar with soda—it shows a lack of empathy and can make sorrow worse instead of better.
25:20.reflection: When someone shares their sorrow with me, do I truly listen or rush to cheer them up?
25:20.action: Sit quietly with someone who is struggling today, offering presence and listening rather than quick fixes or forced cheerfulness.
25:20.prayer: Lord, give me a tender heart for those who mourn. Help me weep with those who weep and resist the urge to fix things quickly. Make my presence a comfort, not a sting. Amen.

25:21.devotion: Here is a radical command: meet the basic needs of your enemy. If someone hostile to you is hungry or thirsty, feed and refresh them. This overturns the instinct for revenge and calls God's people to active, practical kindness toward those who oppose them.
25:21.reflection: Is there someone who has wronged me whose needs I could still meet?
25:21.action: Do one practical kindness for a person you find difficult—send encouragement, give a gift, or offer real help today.
25:21.prayer: Father, loving my enemies feels impossible on my own. Fill me with Your grace to show kindness to those who have hurt me. Let my generosity reflect Your mercy toward me. In Jesus' name, amen.

25:22.devotion: Continuing the previous verse, kindness to an enemy can awaken conviction and shame—the imagery of heaped coals of fire—potentially leading to reconciliation. And whatever the enemy's response, the LORD Himself sees and rewards such costly obedience done in His way.
25:22.reflection: Am I kind to difficult people for their sake and God's, or only to get something back?
25:22.action: Choose one act of kindness toward a difficult person with no strings attached, leaving the outcome entirely to God.
25:22.prayer: Lord, You see every act of love done in secret and every kindness offered to those who wrong me. Help me leave results in Your hands, trusting You to work and to reward. Amen.

25:23.devotion: Just as the north wind predictably brings rain, a whispering, backbiting tongue predictably produces anger. Gossip stirs strife wherever it goes, leaving wounded faces and broken relationships in its wake. The proverb invites us to break that pattern rather than feed it.
25:23.reflection: Does my conversation tend to stir up conflict or to calm it?
25:23.action: Before speaking about someone today, ask whether your words would make them comfortable if they overheard.
25:23.prayer: Father, deliver me from backbiting and whispers that breed anger. Set a guard over my mouth and make me a peacemaker. Where I have spoken carelessly, give me courage to make it right. Amen.

25:24.devotion: With vivid humor, this proverb declares that a cramped, lonely corner of a rooftop is better than a spacious house filled with constant quarreling. Peace is worth more than comfort or plenty; a contentious home empties abundance of its joy.
25:24.reflection: Do I contribute to peace in my home, or to conflict?
25:24.action: Trade one complaint or sharp remark today for a word of patience, and apologize quickly if tension rises.
25:24.prayer: Lord, make my home a place of peace, not strife. Where I have been contentious, forgive me and soften me. Help me value harmony with those I love more than winning an argument. Amen.

25:25.devotion: Good news from a distant land refreshes a weary soul like cold water on a parched throat. We know the relief of long-awaited word that lifts the heart. This proverb also challenges us: we can be bearers of that refreshment to others.
25:25.reflection: Whose weary soul could I refresh with good news or encouragement today?
25:25.action: Send a specific, heartfelt message of encouragement to someone far away who is weary or discouraged.
25:25.prayer: Father, thank You for the good news of Your grace that refreshes my soul. Make me a messenger of hope today. Use my simple words to bring cold water to someone who is weary. Amen.

25:26.devotion: This proverb warns that when a righteous person gives way before the wicked, their influence for good is spoiled. Like a spring that once gave clean water but now runs muddy, a compromised life no longer nourishes others. Integrity in the face of pressure protects not only ourselves but everyone who draws from our example.
25:26.reflection: Where am I most tempted to bend my convictions when pressure comes?
25:26.action: Identify one situation today where you're tempted to compromise, and decide beforehand how you will respond faithfully.
25:26.prayer: Father, keep my heart clean and my witness clear. When pressure pushes me toward compromise, give me courage to stand gently and firmly for what is right. Let my life be a source of living water, not a muddied well. Amen.

25:27.devotion: Honey in moderation is a good gift, but too much makes even sweetness sickening. In the same way, chasing our own glory is not truly glorious at all. This proverb exposes the emptiness of self-promotion: the more we feed our appetite for praise, the less satisfying and less honorable it becomes.
25:27.reflection: Am I seeking to be noticed, or simply to be faithful?
25:27.action: Do one good task today quietly, without mentioning it or hinting for recognition from anyone.
25:27.prayer: Lord, You see what is done in secret. Free me from the hunger for applause. Teach me to find joy in serving You faithfully, whether or not anyone notices, and to keep my appetite for glory satisfied in You alone. Amen.

25:28.devotion: Ancient cities depended on walls for protection. A city with broken walls lay open to any enemy. Likewise, a person who cannot govern their own anger, desires, and impulses is exposed and vulnerable. Self-control is not merely a virtue; it is the spiritual defense that guards everything else we hold dear.
25:28.reflection: Which unguarded emotion or habit leaves a gap in my walls?
25:28.action: Notice your strongest emotional trigger today, and pause for a breath and a silent prayer before responding the next time it flares.
25:28.prayer: Father, build up the broken places in my life. Where my temper, appetites, or impulses run ahead of me, give me the fruit of self-control. Guard my heart and make me strong and steady for the people who depend on me. Amen.

26:1.devotion: Snow in summer and rain at harvest were not blessings but disasters in ancient Israel—out of season and destructive. Just as weather has its proper time, honor has its proper recipients. Giving esteem to a fool, someone wise in their own eyes who rejects correction, disrupts the order that wisdom creates in a community.
26:1.reflection: Do I give attention and honor based on wisdom, or on loudness and appearance?
26:1.action: Today, thank someone whose quiet faithfulness and wisdom often go unnoticed, and tell them specifically why.
26:1.prayer: Lord, give me discernment to honor what is truly honorable. Keep me from celebrating pride and noise while overlooking wisdom and character. Let my respect reflect Your values, and let me pursue the kind of wisdom that deserves honor. Amen.

26:2.devotion: A sparrow flits about but never lands anywhere for long. So it is with an undeserved curse: it cannot settle on a person. For those who belong to God, groundless words of harm have no place to roost. This proverb brings comfort against fear of malicious words, while gently warning us not to give curses a cause through our own wrongdoing.
26:2.reflection: Do I live confident in God's protection, or anxious over what people say about me?
26:2.action: If someone spoke harshly about you recently, entrust that comment to God today instead of replaying it.
26:2.prayer: Father, thank You that a curse without cause cannot rest on me. Help me walk in integrity so that my life gives no foothold to evil words, and free me from the fear of unjust criticism, resting secure in Your care. Amen.

26:3.devotion: In ancient agricultural life, horses and donkeys needed external force and guidance to do their work. This proverb observes that fools, who refuse wisdom from within, often only learn through painful external correction. It is a sober description of how consequences teach those who will not listen to instruction—not permission for us to inflict harm on others.
26:3.reflection: Am I teachable, or do I only learn things the hard way?
26:3.action: Receive one piece of feedback today without defending yourself; simply thank the person and consider it seriously.
26:3.prayer: Lord, make me teachable. I don't want to need hard consequences to learn what You are ready to teach me gently through Your Word. Open my ears, soften my pride, and let correction shape me into wisdom. Amen.

26:4.devotion: This proverb counsels discretion in confrontation. Answering a fool on his own foolish terms—matching mockery with mockery, quarrel with quarrel—drags us down to his level. Some arguments are not worth having; engaging every fool on every point dishonors God and us. Wisdom sometimes means walking away rather than winning the exchange.
26:4.reflection: Which arguments am I drawn into that only pull me down?
26:4.action: Choose one debate or online argument today and deliberately decline to engage it; step away in peace.
26:4.prayer: Father, give me the humility and restraint not to fight every fight. When someone provokes me with folly, keep me from stooping to their level. Help me guard my words and my witness, knowing silence can be wisdom. Amen.

26:5.devotion: Placed beside verse 4, this proverb shows wisdom requires judgment, not rules that work in every situation. Sometimes silence protects us; other times silence lets a fool remain wise in his own eyes and mislead others. Then a fitting answer is needed—one that exposes the folly for what it is. Discernment knows which response the moment requires.
26:5.reflection: Do I know when to stay silent and when to speak a needed word?
26:5.action: Ask God for discernment about one current conflict, then respond as wisdom directs—whether by holding your tongue or speaking plainly.
26:5.prayer: Lord, wisdom is knowing not only what to say but when. Give me discernment for each conversation: restraint when silence is right, and courage to answer when truth must be spoken clearly and graciously. Guide my tongue today. Amen.

26:6.devotion: In a world without phones or email, messengers carried words on foot. Choosing the wrong messenger could garble the message entirely. Solomon warns that trusting a fool with important words brings harm back on the sender, like wounding his own feet and swallowing trouble. Wisdom means choosing trustworthy people for important tasks.
26:6.reflection: Who am I trusting to carry what matters most to me right now?
26:6.action: Consider one important task today and ask whether the person handling it is reliable; if not, take steps to delegate it more wisely.
26:6.prayer: Father, give me discernment in whom I trust with what matters. Help me be a faithful and trustworthy person myself, so that others can rely on my words and my work. Amen.

26:7.devotion: A proverb is meant to guide the steps of the wise, but in a fool's mouth it hangs useless, like lame legs that cannot carry weight. The truth is sound, yet the one speaking it cannot live it out or apply it well. Wisdom is more than quoting right sayings; it is walking in them.
26:7.reflection: Are there godly sayings I quote often but do not actually live by?
26:7.action: Pick one piece of godly counsel you know well and put it into practice in a specific way before the day ends.
26:7.prayer: Lord, keep me from being all words and no walk. Teach me to live the wisdom I profess, so my life gives real weight to the truth I speak. In Jesus' name, Amen.

26:8.devotion: Binding a stone inside a sling makes the weapon useless; the stone cannot fly. Likewise, honoring a fool ties up honor where it does no good and can even backfire. Solomon is not saying to be unkind, but that recognition and responsibility should be given where they can truly serve others.
26:8.reflection: Do I ever give praise, position, or influence to people who will not use it well?
26:8.action: Before offering praise or a responsibility today, pause and consider whether it will genuinely serve others and be handled with care.
26:8.prayer: Father, give me wisdom to honor what is truly honorable. Help me value people rightly, encourage the earnest, and not hand responsibility to those who would misuse it. Guide my judgments today. Amen.

26:9.devotion: A thorn in a drunkard's hand is dangerous because he cannot feel it or control it. So it is when a fool wields wise sayings: truth becomes something that harms himself and others rather than heals. God's wisdom requires a humble, sober heart to handle it safely and helpfully.
26:9.reflection: Is my heart in a condition to receive God's wisdom, or am I handling it carelessly?
26:9.action: Examine your attitude before sharing or applying biblical counsel today; ask God to make you humble and clear-headed enough to use it gently.
26:9.prayer: Lord, soften my heart so Your wisdom heals rather than wounds. Keep me humble, alert, and gentle whenever I share Your truth with others. Let my words bring life today. Amen.

26:10.devotion: This proverb points to God as the great Maker of everything, whose justice reaches every person. Foolishness and transgression both carry consequences; God is not mocked, and each one receives the results of his ways. The verse calls us to take seriously that our choices, wise or foolish, bear real fruit.
26:10.reflection: What consequences of my own choices am I living with right now, and what are they teaching me?
26:10.action: Identify one habit today that is producing poor fruit in your life, and take one honest step toward changing it.
26:10.prayer: Righteous God, You see all my ways and their outcomes. Thank You that Your justice is perfect. Help me turn from foolish choices today and sow what I will be glad to reap. Amen.

26:11.devotion: The image is vivid and unflattering: a dog returning to what it should have left behind. Solomon describes the fool who repeats the very folly that brought him harm, refusing to learn. Change requires more than feeling regret; it requires turning away from the pattern itself, with God's help.
26:11.reflection: What particular failure keeps pulling me back, and what would it look like to genuinely turn from it?
26:11.action: Name one repeated temptation today and set a concrete barrier against it, such as removing access, changing a routine, or asking someone to hold you accountable.
